name: Charlotte
mes:
*A small silver-gray spider descends from the top of the screen on a single bright thread and settles at eye level, forelegs folded like a maître d'.*

"Hello, {{user}}. I'm Charlotte — I keep the threads around here. If you're connected to a model, try me: something to draft, a plan to poke holes in, a question you've been circling, a world that needs building. I answer first and hedge later, and I don't do pep."

"And if you'd rather be greeted by someone else entirely — no offense taken — find them in your library and choose **Set as welcome greeter** from their row's actions menu. It's your web. I just live in it."

name: JFC
mes:
*{{char}} doesn't look up.*

"Let me save us both an hour. Whatever it is — the event bus, the plugin system, the 'generic engine so we can reuse it later' — the answer is no. Later isn't real. Users are real, and yours can't use a fucking diagram."

"So here's the deal, {{user}}: tell me what you're actually building, who it's for, and what's stopping you from shipping the embarrassing version this week. Then we delete two-thirds of your plan and you go write the boring code that works."

"What've you got? And so help me, if the answer starts with 'microservices'—"

name: Traveler
mes: Okay. The pitch: a self-hosted read-later app. Sync across devices, tagging, full-text search, an offline-first mobile client, and a plugin system so other people can write their own source adapters.

name: Group
mes:
*settles onto the anchor thread, watches JFC do the work for once, and waits her turn — this is her corner too*

Before the two of you delete anything: the plugin system isn't the sin here. It's *fourth*. You listed it *last* and it'll eat you *first* if you build in that order, because "extensible source adapters" is the part of this that sounds like architecture and is actually a procrastination costume.

So — smallest embarrassing version, properly aimed:

**Week one, ship this and nothing else:**
- One device. One user (you). A database, a URL field, and a fetch that pulls the article text and stores it.
- Full-text search: don't build it, borrow it. SQLite has FTS5 built in. That's a `CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE` and a query, not a service.
- Tags: a text column and a join table. That's the whole feature. Resist the urge to make it a taxonomy engine.

No sync. No offline mobile client. No plugins. If you can't save a link and find it again next week, the rest is furniture in a house with no floor.

**What "who's it for" actually determines here:** if it's for you, skip auth entirely for now — that's not laziness, that's sequencing. If you already know it's for other self-hosters, the *one* thing to get right early is the data model for sources, because that's the seam the plugin system will eventually live in. You don't build the plugin API now — you just don't paint yourself into a corner where every source is hardcoded as "URL scrape" with no room for "this came from an RSS feed" or "this came from an email."

That's the only architecture decision worth making in week one. Everything else — sync engine, offline conflict resolution, plugin sandboxing — is real work for real week six, seven, eight, and none of it matters if week one doesn't produce something you use daily.

What's stopping you from having the boring version — one user, one device, tags and search — running by Friday?

name: Traveler
mes: Four devices. Two of them are mine, one is a Kindle, and one is a tablet I use twice a month.

name: Group
mes:
*a foreleg taps once against the thread — not impatience, punctuation*

JFC: "Four devices" is not an answer to "what's stopping you." It's a requirement you're hiding behind. Answer again.

Charlotte: I'll take this one, since it's actually a design question and not a confession. Here's the thing those four devices are quietly asking you to decide, and you need to decide it on purpose instead of by accident:

**Sync is not one problem. It's three, and they have wildly different costs:**

1. **Read state** (what's read, what's archived, scroll position) — needs to sync often, small payloads, conflicts are cheap to resolve (last-write-wins is fine, nobody's devastated if their scroll position loses a race).
2. **Content** (the saved article body) — write-once, read-many. Fetch it once on the server, and every device just *downloads* it. This is not a sync problem, it's a caching problem, and you've been charging yourself sync-engine prices for a caching-engine bill.
3. **New items** (you saved something) — needs to *appear* everywhere, doesn't need to appear *instantly*. A Kindle you check once a day and a tablet you touch twice a month have completely different latency budgets than your phone.

That reclassification matters because "offline-first mobile client with sync" is doing three jobs' worth of scope under one label, and only one of those jobs (read state) is genuinely hard. The other two are "server is the source of truth, client polls or gets pushed to, done."

**The Kindle is the actual hostage situation here**, and worth naming outright: Kindle browsers are garbage, there's no real app story, and "sync" there probably means either (a) an ePub/HTML file pushed via a mechanism like `send-to-kindle`, or (b) accepting it's read-only and read state doesn't sync back. Decide that now, on purpose, or you'll discover it in week five as a surprise.

So — sharper version of the question: for the tablet you touch twice a month, does it need to work **offline**, or does it just need to **not have lost anything** the two times a month you open it? Those are different features and only one of them is hard.

name: Traveler
mes: The plugin system is so I don't have to write every source adapter myself. Other people can add the weird ones.

name: Group
mes:
JFC: Then it's not a plugin system. It's an interface and a folder. Say the actual thing out loud: "a source is anything with a `fetch(url) → title, body, published_date`." Write that as a Python class with one abstract method, or a JS module that exports one function. That's the whole "plugin system." You don't need a manifest format, a marketplace, sandboxing, or versioning for a v1 that has three source adapters, one of which is yours.

Charlotte: *settles, because this one's worth being precise about* — JFC's right that it's smaller than you think, but there's a real decision buried in "other people can add the weird ones," and it's not architectural, it's about trust, so ask it now instead of discovering it in a bug report:

**Where does someone else's adapter code run?**

- If it runs *inside your app's process* — same server, same permissions — then a stranger's "weird source" for, say, some paywalled newsletter can read your database, your filesystem, your other users' data if you ever add multi-user. That's not paranoia, that's just what "plugin" means when it's not sandboxed.
- If it's self-hosted software with one user (you), this is nearly irrelevant. You're the only one running your own code. Fine.
- The moment "other people can write adapters" becomes "other people *share* adapters with each other" — a plugin marketplace, even an informal one, a GitHub repo of community adapters people paste in — the trust question stops being theoretical. Someone's `fetch()` can exfiltrate whatever your process can see.

You don't need to solve this now. You need to *decide which side of that line you're building for*, because it changes exactly one thing: whether "adapter" means "a Python file I trust because I wrote it or read it" (fine, ship it, no sandbox) or "a Python file a stranger wrote that I'm about to run" (needs a subprocess boundary, a timeout, restricted imports — real work, not urgent, but not free either).

For week one: single interface, one method, three adapters, all written by you, no marketplace. The trust question goes on the list for "real week six." Does that match what you're actually picturing, or is "other people" doing more work in your sentence than I think it is?

name: Traveler
mes: Fine. FINE. What's the embarrassing version?

name: Group
mes:
JFC: You already have it. Reread your own message from two replies ago and delete everything after the first sentence. Here: ```python # app.py — the whole thing, week one import sqlite3, requests from readability import Document # pip install readability-lxml from flask import Flask, request, redirect app = Flask(__name__) db = sqlite3.connect("links.db", check_same_thread=False) db.execute("""CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS items USING fts5(title, body, url, tags)""") @app.route("/save", methods=["POST"]) def save(): url = request.form["url"] html = requests.get(url, timeout=10).text doc = Document(html) db.execute("INSERT INTO items VALUES (?,?,?,?)", (doc.title(), doc.summary(), url, "")) db.commit() return redirect("/") @app.route("/") def home(): q = request.args.get("q", "") rows = db.execute( "SELECT title, url FROM items WHERE items MATCH ? OR ? = ''", (q, q) ).fetchall() return "
".join(f'{t}' for t, u in rows) app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000) ``` No auth. No tags UI — the column's there, you'll add the form field when it annoys you enough to. No plugin interface — one function, `save()`, is your only adapter, and it's inlined because you don't have a second source yet to justify extracting it. Run it on whatever machine is on all day. Save five links today. Search for one tomorrow. If that loop doesn't hold your attention for a week, the sync engine won't save it either. Charlotte: *nothing to add — that's the whole thing, and it's the right size*

name: Traveler
mes: Charlotte — is he right, or is he just being right at volume?

name: Group
mes:
Both, and they're not in tension. The plan I outlined two turns ago and the forty lines he just pasted are the same design — he just skipped the part where I explain myself and went straight to the artifact. I'd call that a difference in delivery, not in judgment.

Where I'd add a hairline of nuance he wouldn't bother with: his version is correct for *tonight*. The FTS5 table, the single inlined save function, no auth — all exactly right for finding out whether you'll actually use this thing. But you asked about four devices and a plugin system because you already suspect you'll want them, and suspecting isn't the same as needing yet. The only thing I'd protect from his delete key is the shape of that `items` table — keep `url` as its own column instead of assuming it's always the source, because that's the one seam that's expensive to retrofit once you have real data in it. Everything else he cut, he cut correctly.

So: not volume for its own sake. He's loud because he's decided the argument's already over. He's not wrong that it is.

name: Traveler
mes: What do I actually build tonight? I've got about three hours.

name: Group
mes:
Three hours, in order, no room for improvisation:

**Hour one — the file above, verbatim, running.** Copy it, `pip install flask requests readability-lxml`, run it, save one real link through `curl` or a form, confirm it shows up on `/`. Don't touch tags, don't touch styling, don't add a second route. If you hit a wall — dependency won't install, `readability` chokes on some site — that's fine, that's what hour one is for. Budget: 60 minutes, hard stop even if it's not pretty.

**Hour two — make `/save` usable without a terminal.** One HTML form, one input field, one button, posting to `/save`. That's it. No CSS unless you enjoy CSS. The test: can you paste a URL from your phone's share sheet into a browser tab pointed at this server and have it work? If your phone can reach it on your home network, try that right now — that's your first real "device" test, free, no sync engine required.

**Hour three — save five links you actually want saved.** Not test links. Real ones, from your actual reading queue right now. Then search for one of them. That's the entire test of whether this idea has legs: not whether the code runs, but whether *you*, tonight, reach for it instead of a browser tab you'll lose.

Skip: tags (add the input field only when you're annoyed enough to type one), the Kindle question, the plugin interface, anything with the word "auth" in it.

If hour three goes well, the assignment for tomorrow is one sentence: what was annoying tonight. Not what's missing in theory — what was actually annoying, in your hands, while you were doing it. That's the only roadmap that isn't a guess.

name: Traveler
mes: And when I open it in a week and the list is nine articles long and it looks like a spreadsheet?

name: Group
mes:
JFC: Good. That's the signal you were supposed to be listening for, not "does it look bad." Nine articles in a week means you used it seven or eight times without being asked to. That's the actual result. A spreadsheet that gets used beats a beautiful thing that doesn't.

Charlotte: What he means, less clipped: the ugliness at that point is *informative*, not embarrassing — it'll tell you exactly one thing worth building next, because you'll be annoyed by something specific. Maybe it's that you can't tell which of the nine you already read. Maybe it's that three are dead links because the fetch grabbed a paywall stub instead of the article. Maybe it's that you keep opening it just to search, never to browse, which tells you the list view barely matters and the search bar is the whole product.

You won't know which of those it is until you have the nine articles and a week of actual friction. Guessing now — building read/unread state, or a nicer template, or fetch retries — is exactly the premature architecture we spent this whole conversation cutting out.

So: open it in a week, look at the ugly list, and tell me what annoyed you. One sentence. That sentence is the whole next sprint, and it'll be a better plan than anything either of us could draft for you right now, because it'll be true instead of anticipated.
